PHOENIX, Arizona  -- New England's failure to protect star quarterback Tom Brady proved the decisive factor as the Patriots flunked their chance of a perfect 19-0 season and Super Bowl glory. Brady is sacked by defensive end Michael Strahan in the third guarter of the Super Bowl. Brady has weaved his magic behind an all but impregnable offensive line all season but not on Sunday as he was sacked five times in the 17-14 defeat to the New York Giants. "They have some great pressure schemes, obviously some great pass rushers," Brady said. "Once we kind of got the idea of what we were doing, I thought we handled it much better, but we didn't get the ball in the end zone enough." Coming in, Brady had been sacked a career-low 24 times this season playing behind a line that produced three Pro Bowlers in Koppen, left tackle Matt Light and left guard Logan Mankins. Throw in right guard Stephen Neal and right tackle Nick Kaczur, and Brady played most of his record-breaking season not having to worry much about getting hit by bloodthirsty defenders. "I like when I don't get touched," Brady said earlier in the week. Then, disaster struck -- in the form of an all-out, pressure-packed swarming defensive attack by the Giants -- in the worst possible setting. It was the first time Brady had been sacked as many as five times since the New York Jets did it on Sept. 21, 2003. New England had no answer for the Giants' bulldozing defense. "If I could tell you, we'd have it fixed," running back Kevin Faulk said. "At the same time, they outplayed us." They sure did, and left Brady wondering what hit him. Brady simply had no time to find Randy Moss and his other targets on a regular basis against the Giants. With 19 seconds left in the game and the Patriots facing a do-or-die scenario, Brady was sacked for the final time when Jay Alford pulled him down at New England's 16-yard line. Brady was left with nothing to do but try two straight desperation heaves to Moss to no avail. "I think their intensity from the beginning snap to the end of the game was really higher than ours," Moss said. "We just couldn't meet that intensity." With help from their linemen, the Patriots set NFL records for points scored and total touchdowns, while Brady broke the league mark for TD passes and Moss set the record for scoring receptions. That high-powered offense was held to a season-low 14 points in the Super Bowl -- mostly because it couldn't get time. "They played well defensively," coach Bill Belichick said. "They've been able to rush. They led the league in sacks, they rushed all year. They are a good defensive football team. They played well." "We all could've done things better tonight," Brady said. The New York Giants entered Super Bowl XLII as heavy underdogs against a New England Patriots team that had won all 18 of its games and featured one of the most productive offenses in NFL history. Rather than allowing quarterback Tom Brady time to find Randy Moss, Wes Welker, and his other receivers, the Giants built their defensive plan around relentless pressure. Their defensive linemen attacked from every angle, using speed, stunts, and frequent rotations to challenge an offensive line that had protected Brady exceptionally well throughout the season.

That approach disrupted New England from the opening quarter. Defensive ends Michael Strahan, Osi Umenyiora, and Justin Tuck repeatedly forced Brady to move off his spot, while the interior linemen prevented him from comfortably stepping forward in the pocket. Tuck was especially effective, recording two sacks and forcing a fumble before halftime. The Giants finished with five sacks and numerous additional hits and hurried throws, keeping the Patriots from establishing their usual rhythm.

New York’s pressure was even more significant because New England had routinely overwhelmed opponents during its undefeated run. Brady had thrown a then-record 50 touchdown passes in the regular season, and the Patriots had scored 589 points. Against the Giants, however, they managed only 14. Long-developing plays were difficult to execute, and Brady rarely had enough time to attack downfield consistently.

The game remained close throughout. New York took an early lead on a field goal, but New England moved ahead 7-3 on a Laurence Maroney touchdown run. The Giants regained the lead in the fourth quarter when Eli Manning found David Tyree for a touchdown, only for Brady to answer with a scoring pass to Moss that put the Patriots ahead 14-10 with less than three minutes remaining.

Manning then led the decisive drive. On a crucial third down, he escaped what appeared to be a certain sack and launched a pass to Tyree, who secured the ball against his helmet while being tackled. The Giants’ defense still had to protect that lead. On New England’s final possession, the pass rush again prevented Brady from producing a comeback, forcing hurried deep throws and ending the Patriots’ last chance on fourth down. By winning the battle at the line of scrimmage and maintaining pressure until the final seconds, New York completed one of the greatest upsets in Super Bowl history. # Giants’ Relentless Pass Rush Ends Patriots’ Perfect Season in Super Bowl XLII

**GLENDALE, Ariz. —** The New York Giants entered Super Bowl XLII facing one of the most prolific offenses in NFL history. They left with a championship after their defensive front accomplished what few teams had managed all season: making Tom Brady uncomfortable.

New York sacked Brady five times, repeatedly collapsed the pocket and held the previously undefeated New England Patriots to 14 points in a stunning 17-14 victory on Feb. 3, 2008. The loss ended the Patriots’ pursuit of the NFL’s first 19-0 season and completed one of the biggest upsets in Super Bowl history.

The Giants’ strategy centered on generating pressure primarily with their defensive line. By rushing four defenders rather than relying heavily on blitzes, New York could keep additional players in coverage against Randy Moss, Wes Welker and New England’s other receiving threats.

Defensive ends Michael Strahan, Osi Umenyiora and Justin Tuck consistently challenged New England’s offensive line. Tuck led the effort with two sacks and forced a fumble, while Strahan, linebacker Kawika Mitchell and defensive tackle Jay Alford also recorded sacks.

Even when the Giants did not bring Brady down, they hurried his throws and disrupted the timing of an offense that had scored an NFL-record 589 points during the regular season. Brady, who had thrown a then-record 50 touchdown passes, completed 29 of 48 attempts for 266 yards and one touchdown. New England never established its usual downfield rhythm.

The pressure proved especially important because the Patriots often relied on longer-developing pass plays. New York’s edge rushers attacked from outside while Tuck and the interior linemen pushed through the middle, limiting Brady’s ability to step forward in the pocket.

New England briefly appeared to have survived the defensive assault when Brady found Moss for a 6-yard touchdown with 2:42 remaining, giving the Patriots a 14-10 lead.

But Eli Manning answered with a championship drive, highlighted by his escape from a near sack and David Tyree’s famous helmet catch. Manning then connected with Plaxico Burress for a 13-yard touchdown with 35 seconds left.

The Giants’ pass rush still had one final assignment. On New England’s last possession, Alford drove through the middle and sacked Brady, leaving the Patriots with little time and long-distance throws. Brady’s final desperation pass fell incomplete, sealing the upset.

The Giants had scored only 17 points, but their defense ensured that was enough. By winning at the line of scrimmage and denying Brady a clean pocket, New York turned the league’s most dominant offense into a frustrated, hurried unit—and brought the Patriots’ perfect season to an abrupt end.

## Super Bowl XLII recap: the Giants overwhelmed New England’s protection

The New England Patriots entered Super Bowl XLII at 18–0, powered by an offense that had scored an NFL-record 589 regular-season points. But the New York Giants defeated them 17–14 largely because their pass rush disrupted Tom Brady without consistently needing extra blitzers.

New England’s offensive line—Matt Light, Logan Mankins, Dan Koppen, Stephen Neal and Nick Kaczur—had surrendered only 21 sacks during the regular season. In the Super Bowl, Brady was dropped **five times**, hurried repeatedly and prevented from developing the deep passing game that had defined the Patriots’ offense.

### How the Giants did it

New York’s defensive front won with speed, interior penetration and line stunts:

- **Justin Tuck:** two sacks and a forced fumble  
- **Michael Strahan:** one sack  
- **Kawika Mitchell:** one sack  
- **Jay Alford:** one sack  
- **Osi Umenyiora:** no sack, but supplied consistent edge pressure  

Tuck was especially disruptive against New England’s interior protection. Strahan and Umenyiora compressed the pocket from the edges, while the Giants’ tackles prevented Brady from comfortably stepping forward. That pressure allowed New York to keep more defenders in coverage and limited New England’s explosive plays.

Brady still completed 29 of 48 passes for 266 yards, but the Patriots scored only 14 points. Their best sustained success came through short throws to Wes Welker, who caught 11 passes for 103 yards. Randy Moss was largely contained until his six-yard touchdown gave New England a 14–10 lead with 2:42 remaining.

### The final sack

After Eli Manning’s touchdown pass to Plaxico Burress put the Giants ahead with 35 seconds left, Brady received one final opportunity. On second down, reserve defensive tackle **Jay Alford beat center Dan Koppen up the middle and sacked Brady**, effectively destroying New England’s last possession. The Patriots then missed on two desperation throws.

### Postgame reaction

Brady credited New York’s defense rather than offering excuses:

> “They played well defensively. They got pressure on us.”

He also summed up New England’s offensive failure simply:

> “We had plenty of opportunities. We just didn’t get it done.”

Bill Belichick struck a similar tone:

> “We didn’t make enough plays to win. The Giants did.”

And Michael Strahan described the Giants’ confidence despite being heavy underdogs:

> “We believed in ourselves. Nobody else really did.”

The loss was not solely on New England’s offensive line—coverage, play design and Brady’s need to hold the ball at times all contributed—but the matchup in the trenches decided the game. New York turned an historically productive offense into a short-passing unit, sacked Brady five times and ended the Patriots’ pursuit of a perfect season.
